title: One action at a time
hookLine: build your life action by action; no one can stop you doing each well (Meditations 8.32)
tomorrow: Not the whole life at once

lines: A LIFE BUILT THE SAME WAY.
cards: A stone wall on an old farm. No mortar, no blueprint. Somebody built it by picking up one stone, turning it until it fit, setting it down, and picking up the next.
When a stone was too big, they didn't quit; they set it aside and found one that fit the gap. Generations later, the wall still stands.
Marcus Aurelius thought a life gets built the same way, and this part of the path takes its title from today's entry.

teach.h: BUILD YOUR LIFE ACTION BY ACTION.
teach.b: In Meditations eight, thirty-two, Marcus says you have to put your life together action by action, and if each action does its job as far as it can, be satisfied. Not each life. Each action.
That's the unit. Then something bold: no one can stop you from making each action do its job. Someone might object that some outside thing will get in the way.

teach.h: NO ONE CAN STOP YOU ACTING WELL.
teach.b: Marcus answers: nothing can stop you acting justly, with self-control and with good sense. The world can block your plans; it can't block the way you meet the block. Then the most practical part.
Maybe something stops the particular action you intended. Fine.

Accept the obstacle gracefully, turn to what is possible, and a new action takes its place, one that fits the same building. That's the farmer setting aside the stone that's too big. The wall keeps rising.
And this frees you. If your life is one giant project, every setback threatens the whole thing.

teach.h: THE NEXT STONE IS ALWAYS THERE.
teach.b: Built action by action, a setback is just one stone that didn't fit, and the next stone is always there.
You don't need to fix your whole life today, only do the next action well. Marcus wrote it for an emperor's days. It fits a stack of laundry just as well.

how: Readers of Marcus often treat their day as a series of single actions to do well, and when a plan is blocked, they accept it and choose the next possible action rather than abandoning the whole.

o: a Greek mason who taught philosophy with stones
the emperor who said build a life action by action
a Roman general who built walls on the frontier

games.q: one action at a time — tap the pairs.
p: each action, not the whole life
built one stone at a time

s: Marcus says outside things can stop you acting justly
he says nothing can stop you acting justly, with self-control and good sense.
8.32 says when one action is blocked, another can take its place
accept the obstacle, turn to what's possible, and a new action fits the building.

games.q: your plan for the afternoon is blocked by something you can't change. what does Marcus do?
o: accept the obstacle and do the next possible action well.
keep pushing at the blocked plan.
games.why: Meditations 8.32: accept the hindrance, turn to what's allowed, and another action takes its place that fits the building of your life.

practice: Don't think about your whole life, or even your whole day. Ask only: what is the very next action I'll take after this sit, standing up, making a call, washing a cup, and how would I do it well?
If your mind jumps ahead to the rest of the list, set the list down and come back to the next stone.

wordCard.voice: Marcus, who said a life is put together action by action, and when one is blocked, another that fits takes its place. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: an action, a deed, something done.

carryVoice: Your line: pick up the next stone. The wall rises one fit at a time. That's day six hundred one.
